title: σ-algebras and measurable functions
summary: Why a measure cannot live on every subset; σ-algebras and their countable operations; generated and Borel σ-algebras; measurable functions through preimages of open sets, the (α, ∞] criterion, closure under algebraic operations and countable limits; simple functions and the dyadic approximation theorem.

objectives.description: State the σ-algebra axioms, derive closure under countable intersections and differences, and decide with proof whether a given collection (power set, countable–co-countable, finite–cofinite) is a σ-algebra.
Prove that the σ-algebra generated by a collection exists, describe it explicitly for a finite partition, and define the Borel σ-algebra of a topological space.
Prove the (α, ∞] criterion for measurability and use it to show that sums, products, suprema, infima and pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable.
Prove that every nonnegative measurable function is the pointwise limit of an increasing sequence of measurable simple functions, and say where the convergence is uniform.

preparation.description: Read lecture 1 (3 PDF pages): the σ-algebra axioms and their contrast with a topology, the definition of a measurable function, Proposition 0.1, Theorem 0.2 with its proof, Examples (a)–(d), Proposition 0.3 and Borel sets.
Read lecture 2, PDF pages 1–2: Proposition 0.1 (the preimage σ-algebra, Borel preimages, the (α, ∞] criterion), lim sup and lim inf, Theorem 0.3 and Corollary 0.4.
Read lecture 2, PDF page 3 as far as Theorem 0.5: f^+ and f^-, simple functions and the dyadic approximation theorem. Stop before the definition of a positive measure, which opens unit 2.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A σ-algebra is closed under arbitrary unions, like a topology.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Only countable unions are required, and deliberately so: a σ-algebra on ℝ containing the singletons and closed under arbitrary unions would be all of P(ℝ), and unit 5 shows that no translation-invariant extension of length exists on P(ℝ).

commonMisconceptions.claim: The composition of two measurable functions is measurable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The theorem is continuous-after-measurable (lecture 1, Proposition 0.1(2)), and Borel-after-measurable holds by lecture 2, Proposition 0.1(b). Measurable-after-measurable and measurable-after-continuous can fail once there are Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel (unit 5).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Checking {f > α} for every real α is weaker than checking the preimage of every open set.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It is equivalent: the collection of sets with measurable preimage is a σ-algebra and the rays (α, ∞] generate the open sets of [−∞, ∞] (lecture 2, Proposition 0.1). Rational α even suffice (exercise 2).

commonMisconceptions.claim: The supremum of any family of measurable functions is measurable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Theorem 0.3 is about sequences: {sup_n f_n > α} is a countable union. For an uncountable family the supremum can fail to be measurable; the indicator of a non-measurable set (unit 5) is the supremum of the indicators of its points.

checks.name: source-locators
checks.evidence: All ten statement-level locators point into lecture PDFs 1 and 2, downloaded and text-extracted on 2026-10-30 (3 and 4 pages, no printed labels): σ-algebra axioms and Proposition 0.1 on lecture 1 PDF page 1 (index 0), Theorem 0.2 and Proposition 0.3 on page 2 (index 1), Borel sets on page 3; lecture 2 Proposition 0.1 on page 1, Theorem 0.3 and Corollary 0.4 on page 2, Theorem 0.5 on page 3.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Build agent re-derived: the 2^n count for a partition σ-algebra (distinctness needs nonempty blocks); the case split proving the countable–co-countable collection is a σ-algebra and equals σ(singletons); the finite–cofinite failure via every other point of a countably infinite subset; the rational-test criterion; the characterisation of M_c-measurable functions through the down-set S = {q ∈ ℚ : {f ≤ q} countable} and c = sup S, including why S is nonempty and proper because X is uncountable; the direct limit check in exercise 2 part 3.

checks.name: answer-leakage
checks.evidence: Reference reasoning lives only in instructor/. The lesson names the countable–co-countable example and the finite–cofinite warning without giving the witness, the count or the characterisation; the prompts do not state them either.
